A Rust-first x86-64 operating system built around native domains and Linux userspace compatibility.
Ginux is an independent kernel and operating-system prototype. It boots directly through UEFI without a Linux host kernel, provides its own memory management, scheduler, process model, VFS, networking, device support, and Linux ABI, and runs an embedded administration controller in ring 3. Its primary workload is an unmodified Linux userspace running inside a kernel-native domain .
The repository contains the complete bootable system, controller, native services, Linux compatibility implementation, hardware paths, build tools, architecture specifications, and QEMU test harnesses. The current development target is an x86-64 Q35 virtual machine with OVMF, Intel IOMMU, and virtio devices. It runs through KVM on an x86-64 Linux host and QEMU TCG on Apple Silicon.
build as one bootable GINUX.EFI image;
start its embedded controller as an ordinary ring-3 process;
configure devices, networking, storage, and persistent domain definitions;
pull, verify, cache, and assemble OCI images into domain-local roots;
create and run multiple domains with separate process, address-space, filesystem, mount, capability, and lifecycle state;

boot Rocky Linux 10 systemd through multi-user.target .
Ginux is experimental. Linux ABI coverage, device support, filesystems, networking, resource enforcement, security validation, and real-hardware coverage are incomplete. It is useful for research, architecture experiments, and testing—not production workloads or as a replacement for Linux.
The name is a joke in the same family as Linux: Ginux combines Linux, GPT, and Greg. To keep the author's ego within its configured resource limit, the G officially stands for GPT.
Linux userspace without Linux underneath. Linux is a personality exposed by Ginux, not the host kernel.
Domains as the native system boundary. Domains own processes, address spaces, filesystems, devices, resources, authority, and lifecycle.
A self-contained boot image. The kernel, controller, and core boot requirements ship in one EFI release unit.
A small userspace control plane. The embedded controller configures and observes the kernel without executing in ring 0.
Explicit, revocable authority. Kernel capabilities grant access to named objects and are tied to domain generations for cleanup after failure.
OCI as transport, not runtime. OCI delivers and assembles filesystems; Ginux domains provide execution and isolation.
Compatibility as an observable contract. Real Alpine and Rocky Linux workloads supplement synthetic ABI tests.
UEFI loads one GINUX.EFI image containing the kernel, boot catalog, and authenticated controller payload. Small assembly boundaries enter and leave UEFI, install exception, interrupt, and syscall entries, and switch privilege and address-space state; policy and most mechanisms are implemented in Rust.
The controller is part of the single EFI release unit rather than a service installed in a host distribution. At boot, the kernel maps the statically linked controller into ring 3. It configures the kernel and devices, discovers host state, manages networking and persistent storage, maintains the OCI cache, defines domains, and controls their resources, attachments, autostart, and lifecycle. Ordinary process behavior uses the Linux ABI; protected management operations use a versioned device/ ioctl interface checked by the kernel.
This arrangement keeps the bootable system self-contained without running the controller in ring 0. The controller can delegate or revoke authority granted by the sealed boot envelope, but it cannot create new kernel authority.
A domain is a native Ginux kernel object and the outer unit of isolation, ownership, accounting, scheduling, lifecycle, and failure containment. A domain owns or is granted:
processes, threads, and address spaces;
a generation-tagged capability table;
IPC objects and shared-memory grants;
network endpoints and device grants; and
Domains are stronger boundaries than OCI containers or Linux namespaces. OCI supplies an initial filesystem; Ginux supplies isolation and execution. A single Linux-personality domain can look like a conventional computer, with systemd as PID 1 and a distribution userspace above it. Multiple domains share one Ginux kernel while retaining separate kernel-owned state.
A personality is the userspace contract visible inside a domain: executable format, syscalls, processes, signals, VFS behavior, devices, terminals, clocks, networking, and namespace expectations. Linux x86-64 is the only implemented personality. Other personalities, such as BSD, remain architectural possibilities rather than tested features.
Filesystems, devices, and persistence
The kernel VFS presents domain-local roots assembled from verified OCI layers, a writable overlay, and selected tmpfs , procfs , and devfs behavior. A persistent host-owned volume stores controller configuration and a content-addressed OCI cache across reboots.
The validated QEMU profile includes virtio block and network paths, MSI-X, and VT-d DMA confinement. Measured Rust driver and protocol services can run in separate ring-3 domains with bounded MMIO, DMA, queue, and packet authority. General driver support, production storage guarantees, broad filesystem coverage, and a physical-hardware matrix remain future work.
The validated development target is QEMU's x86-64 Q35 machine with OVMF, Intel IOMMU, and virtio devices. QEMU uses KVM on a suitable x86-64 Linux host and TCG on Apple Silicon Macs.
The Linux 6.12 x86-64 ledger classifies all 375 syscall numbers: 82 complete, 245 partial, and 48 policy-denied. Classification means every syscall number has an explicit disposition; it does not mean complete Linux conformance. Loader, process, VFS, terminal, socket, IPC, namespace, cgroup, pseudo-filesystem, and device behavior is implemented only to the extent recorded in the compatibility matrix .
The project uses real workloads as compound integration tests. Alpine exercises the musl/BusyBox path. Rocky exercises glibc, dynamic linking, fork/exec, systemd, services, procfs, terminals, and related kernel interfaces. A successful tested workflow is evidence for that workflow only; it is not a guarantee that an arbitrary Linux binary or distribution will run.

skills contains portable HDAE development and scheduled PR/issue review Agent Skills shared by Codex and Claude Code.
The canonical skills live under skills/ . Git-tracked relative symlinks expose the same files to Codex under .agents/skills/ and to Claude Code under .claude/skills/ . Start a new agent session from this repository after checking out the branch that contains those links so the agent discovers them at startup.
Use this skill when starting or restructuring substantial work. It begins with focused Q&A, helps the human establish product intent and architecture, creates milestones with executable gates, and gives the agent autonomy to iterate inside each approved gate. It stops at gate boundaries for human direction.
In Claude Code, use the same request with the Claude skill command:
The user may begin with only an idea. The agent is responsible for eliciting the structured project brief through focused follow-up questions, confirming it, and writing it into durable project state before implementation. The skill also requires the agent to propose complete gates, ask what is missing, wait for approval, and update the persisted status at every stopping point. After approving a gate, tell the agent to implement that named gate using the same skill.
Use this skill to establish read-only reviews of new or updated GitHub issues and pull requests. The agent discovers the repository, checks for a connected GitHub account or authenticated gh CLI, guides installation or interactive login when needed, and asks for the frequency, time/day anchor, timezone, scope, report destination, and notification preference. It validates access with a review before creating the schedule.
Codex can use its native recurring automation when available. Claude Code uses an available native scheduler or proposes an explicit repository workflow or host scheduler for approval. In either environment, the skill verifies that the unattended runtime can access the repository before creating the task; it never asks for a token to be pasted into the conversation.
Ginux was built to test whether a coding agent, directed by someone with the relevant systems experience, could construct an independent kernel that runs existing Linux userspace. Over eleven days, one persistent OpenAI Codex task using GPT-5.6 Sol produced approximately 139,000 retained lines of implementation and test code.
The development method is called Human-Directed Agentic Engineering (HDAE) . Human direction established the architecture, constraints, milestones, acceptance criteria, and stopping point. The agent implemented, booted, tested, diagnosed, and revised the system against executable gates. Architecture and decision documents kept the work aligned; real userspaces exposed failures that synthetic tests missed.
The result demonstrates rapid construction of deep systems software, not a production alternative to Linux. The project does not reproduce Linux's broad compatibility, hardware enablement, review, vendor ecosystem, community, or long-term maintenance.
